entry.title: Shippable Governance and the Human in the Loop
entry.summary: Over the past several months, I dove headfirst into the emerging practice of working with autonomous coding agents. entry.content:
Over the past several months, I dove headfirst into the emerging practice of working with autonomous coding agents. In the broader cultural zeitgeist, people have started calling this “vibe coding”: describing a mode where you casually prompt a language model, lean back, and watch working software materialize on the screen.

The experience is intoxicating. Seeing ideas translate into running systems within minutes provides an immediate, compounding feedback loop. I found myself rewiring entire operational patterns across my daily work, from managing deep research dossiers and complex academic coursework down to automating household logistics and personal errands. Tasks that previously required an afternoon of manual scaffolding now execute in seconds.

Yet the moment you move past trivial scripts and attempt to build durable software systems with these tools, the naive dream of effortless automation collides with reality.

Working with an ecosystem of autonomous agents does not feel like operating a compiler, a code generator, or a spreadsheet. It feels strikingly, unmistakably like coaching an engineering delivery team.

You assign an objective, observe the execution, and inspect the resulting output. When something breaks, you step in with diagnostic questions that any seasoned engineering leader would recognize: What was your foundation for that design? What sources did you lean on? Did you verify whether that dependency actually exists, or did you assume it was there because it sounded plausible?

Working across multiple models, reasoning engines, and subagents exposes the reality of cognitive diversity in machines. One model is brilliant at creative architectural synthesis but prone to silent drift if left unmonitored. Another is pedantically literal, executing instructions with surgical precision while missing obvious systemic context. A third model hallucinates libraries with cheerful confidence unless pinned to deterministic schemas. Coaxing consistent, high-integrity outcomes from this ensemble requires constant calibration, coaching, and boundary setting.

The initial temptation for any practitioner discovering these quirks is to micro-manage the system. You configure the software to prompt you for permission before every single tool invocation, file edit, or terminal command.

That instinct is a trap. Sitting in front of a computer screen manually approving dozens of routine function calls reduces a seasoned professional to a stressed-out clerk. You spend your day clicking “Approve” on shell commands you barely have time to read, introducing massive cognitive latency while achieving zero genuine safety. You end up doing almost nothing useful, exhausted by the illusion of control.

If you cannot micro-manage every move, and you cannot let autonomous agents run wild without boundaries, how do you govern them?

The answer is the same answer that great engineering leaders discovered decades ago when scaling human organizations: you stop acting like a manual gatekeeper, and you start shipping the rules as code.

The Gatekeeper Dilemma
#

Years ago, while leading delivery modernization initiatives in central banking, I found myself sitting in an enterprise architecture review board that had become an immovable institutional bottleneck.

Teams across the bank spent months building digital capabilities, only to have their initiatives held in limbo for weeks waiting for an architecture committee to convene, debate, and render judgment. Project managers were exasperated; business sponsors were furious. When I challenged the committee on the multi-week backlog, the chair explained that their rigorous manual review was the only barrier standing between the bank and catastrophic systemic failure.

I proposed a straightforward alternative: “Tell us the exact criteria you use to evaluate these systems. Write them down as explicit principles and automated checks. We will embed those checks directly into the delivery pipelines so teams can prove compliance before they ever ask for time on your calendar.”

The response was immediate, visceral, and revealing.

“Why would we do that?” a senior architect replied. “If we give you the criteria upfront, you will just design the project so that it passes.”

I sat in silence for a moment, waiting for him to recognize the irony. He did not. In his mental model, governance was not an engineering standard to be met; it was a personal interrogation. If a delivery team knew the rules in advance and engineered their system to satisfy every one of them, the committee felt cheated of its sovereign prerogative to pass judgment.

That exchange exposed the fundamental dysfunction of traditional gatekeeping. When organizations treat review criteria as proprietary secrets guarded by a designated priesthood, governance ceases to be a mechanism for quality and becomes a mechanism for control. Delivery teams are forced to guess what the committee wants, while gatekeepers preserve their institutional relevance through arbitrary post-hoc inspection.

The tragedy of this dynamic is that it damages both sides. Delivery teams view governance as an adversarial tax to be evaded whenever possible. Meanwhile, the gatekeepers carry an exhausting emotional burden, convinced that the entire organization will collapse unless they personally inspect every line of documentation.

The Mechanics of Bounded Autonomy
#

The lesson from my laptop running coding agents is the exact lesson from the central banking boardroom: you cannot govern autonomous actors through manual tollbooths. You govern them by constructing an operational environment of bounded autonomy.

To let an autonomous agent run fast without wrecking the environment, you do not hover over its shoulder. You engineer the platform so that unsafe operations are mechanically impossible.

In our agentic engineering practice, that meant wiring up explicit technical guardrails:

First, we isolated capabilities using the Model Context Protocol (MCP). Instead of giving an agent broad, untracked shell access, we expose domain-specific tools with clear schemas. An agent tasked with querying data can access local SQLite tables, but it holds no permission to modify the schema or delete records without dedicated review paths.

Second, we installed deterministic pre-flight hooks. Before any code is committed or any document is published, automated scripts scan the work. If an agent introduces banned security patterns, unverified credentials, or corporate filler language, the hook fails immediately with a descriptive error. The agent receives immediate feedback from the system, adjusts its output, and tries again without human intervention.

Third, we separated drafting from verification. We established multi-stage review patterns: an agent that drafts a proposal is not allowed to approve it. A separate reviewer agent, loaded with an adversarial prompt, challenges the assertions, checks calculations against raw source dossiers, and flags unearned assumptions.

When these guardrails are in place, the entire dynamic shifts. I no longer sit watching terminal output with white knuckles. I can assign a complex, multi-stage task, step away, and return to find work that has already passed dozens of deterministic quality checks. Autonomy is unlocked because the boundaries are absolute.

The Vulnerability of Codification
#

If shifting governance into automated guardrails is so effective, why do so many organizations resist it?

They resist it because codifying evaluation standards into explicit, testable rules is demanding intellectual work that forces professionals into uncomfortable vulnerability.

Much of what an experienced architect, security officer, or compliance lead considers “judgment” is actually tacit pattern recognition accumulated over decades of operational firefighting. Translating that intuition into unambiguous, written requirements forces reviewers to confront their own assumptions. It requires them to separate genuine, non-negotiable architectural constraints from personal aesthetic preferences and historical corporate folklore.

Worse, codification introduces professional vulnerability. As long as standards remain vague and unwritten, a reviewer can never be proven wrong. They can reject an initiative based on an unarticulated sense that something “does not feel enterprise-ready,” safe in the knowledge that no one can audit their reasoning. The moment a committee commits its rules to paper, those rules can be debated, measured, and challenged.

Most threatening of all, once review criteria are codified into explicit rules, those rules can be automated.

This is the psychological threshold where traditional oversight clashes with modern engineering. If an automated suite can verify data classification schemas, boundary protections, cryptographic standards, and identity assertions in five seconds, the traditional two-hour review meeting loses its justification. Gatekeepers sense this intuitively. They resist open criteria because they fear that publishing the rulebook renders the referee obsolete.

In an agentic environment, however, hoarding criteria is fatal. Language models and autonomous agents cannot read minds, navigate political subtext, or divine unwritten corporate norms. If you feed an agentic system vague aspirations and expect it to guess what a committee will approve three weeks later, the system will fail every time. High-velocity automation demands radical transparency of constraints. If a standard cannot be written down and verified, it remains an institutional mood without operational standing.

Shifting from Tollbooths to Guardrails
#

The only path to scaling autonomous systems safely is to invert the control structure. We must shift governance from post-hoc manual inspection into shippable, executable guardrails.

In traditional software delivery, this pattern is already familiar as shift-left testing. Decades ago, testing was an isolated phase conducted by a separate quality assurance department after developers declared their code complete. Work was tossed over a wall; defects were logged weeks later; schedules slipped indefinitely. Modern engineering resolved that paralysis by bringing automated unit tests, integration suites, and security scans directly into the developer workflow. Quality became an automated property of the build, freeing delivery teams from quarterly committee approvals.

Agentic systems require an identical inversion, but applied across an operational canvas that encompasses reasoning, language, and tool invocation.

Governance cannot be an event that occurs after an agent finishes generating artifacts. Governance must be the operational scaffold within which the agent operates. This is the core thesis behind emerging frameworks like Gartner AI Trust, Risk, and Security Management (AI TRiSM): model safety and operational integrity cannot rely on static pre-deployment audits. They require continuous runtime validation, dynamic authorization barriers, and deterministic circuit breakers.

When organizations ship governance as code, compliance becomes frictionless. The delivery team does not wonder whether their work will pass the committee; they know it passes because the automated test suite green-lit the build. The adversarial tension between delivery and oversight dissolves. The rules are open, deterministic, and objective.

The Exploratory Validator
#

When an organization successfully inverts its controls and ships executable guardrails, an immediate question arises: what happens to the human in the loop?

If deterministic suites verify syntax, test execution, schema compliance, and formatting, does the human disappear?

The answer is an emphatic no. The difference is that the human’s role undergoes a qualitative transformation. The human stops serving as a manual gatekeeper performing repetitive compliance checks; the human becomes an exploratory validator.

Consider the reality of testing in an agentic development environment. A deterministic test suite can easily prove that a document contains no banned words, that all cross-references resolve to existing files, that mathematical formulas balance, and that visual components compile without syntax errors. Those checks are binary, objective, and fast. An automated system can execute fifty of them in parallel without breaking stride.

Yet an automated suite cannot tell you whether an essay has struck the right emotional register for an anxious board of directors. It cannot tell you that an interactive diagram, while technically valid, conveys an ambiguous metaphor that will confuse non-technical executives. It cannot tell you that an automated script, while perfectly fulfilling its literal prompt, is optimizing for a local metric that damages the broader strategic goal.

Only an active human, engaging with the system’s output with genuine curiosity and operational context, catches those anomalies.

This is the true role of the human in an autonomous workflow. The human does not sit between step three and step four rubber-stamping routine calculations. The human interacts with the synthesized work, probes its boundaries, tests its real-world interfaces, and inspects the unexpected seams where codified rules fall short. The exploratory validator tests not only the application, but the guardrails themselves against real-world ambiguity.

When the human discovers an unexpected failure mode, they do not simply patch the immediate symptom and move on. They do the real work of engineering: they extract the lesson and encode it back into the automated test suite.

If an agentic draft repeatedly adopts a patronizing tone when addressing regulatory auditors, the human does not manually rewrite the paragraphs forever. The human writes a new linter check, updates the system prompt constraints, and adds the failure case to the automated evaluation suite. The human’s judgment is leveraged: a single exploratory insight permanently improves every future execution of the system.

In this architecture, human involvement is the primary engine of systemic learning. The machine provides flawless execution of codified rules; the human provides the requisite variety necessary to absorb environmental complexity and explore the uncodified frontier.

Pocket-Ready Rules
#

Building high-velocity autonomous systems requires abandoning both the myth of the unattended loop and the security blanket of the bureaucratic tollbooth. For leaders navigating this transition, five operational maxims establish the baseline:

If a rule cannot be written as an automated check, it remains an unverified aspiration.

Engineering designs systems to pass defined constraints; withholding the criteria preserves bureaucratic control.

Manual inspection of routine automated outputs produces review fatigue and rubber stamps, never safety.

The human in the loop functions as an exploratory validator of edge cases, leaving predictable transactions to deterministic code.

Every manual intervention that does not result in a new codified guardrail is technical debt paid in human attention.

entry.title: Difference Needs Somewhere to Go
entry.summary: I was raised up believing I was somehow unique. Like a snowflake distinct among snowflakes. Unique in each way you’d conceive. And now after some thinking I’d say I’d rather be, a functioning cog in some great machinery, serving something beyond me. Opening lyrics to…
entry.content:
I was raised up believing I was somehow unique. Like a snowflake distinct among snowflakes. Unique in each way you’d conceive. And now after some thinking I’d say I’d rather be, a functioning cog in some great machinery, serving something beyond me.

Opening lyrics to Helplessness Blues by Fleet Foxes

At about twenty-five, I was in my first real job, working on a major project. We were on the cusp of a complex, multi-million-dollar initiative, about to scale from a business-case team of five into a delivery operation of more than fifty. On my way to work every day, I listened to music on a ten-minute walk. I rarely got through more than the first few tracks of an album before arriving, saying hello, and starting my day.

When Helplessness Blues came out, the title track stuck with me. I had never heard “being a cog in a machine” used as anything other than an insult, but here it was presented as a relief. In the right machine, you could contribute to something far better than anything you could build alone. The idea of being a unique snowflake as an exhausting, solitary burden had never crossed my mind before.

As our project grew, my place on a small team where relationships were tight and personal came to an end. On that small team, we had the time to see each other as people. We knew our quirks, and could see where a colleague’s former experience in finance, a talent for trivia, or a knack for storytelling was far more valuable than any job description could capture.

Moving from that tight-knit group to my first large-scale project brought an anxious transition. I did not know where I was supposed to fit, or what cog I was supposed to be in what machine. I could feel a shift in the room from a dynamic where the right answer emerged from discussion to one where the right answer came from hierarchy. I was unsure where our differences fit when truth was no longer found through debate, but dictated by a spot on an organizational chart.

Throughout my career, that tension kept returning: When to bring more of myself into the room. When to make space for someone else. How to contribute to something larger without assuming that contribution requires leaving individuality at the door.

Having been away from work for a while, I find myself preparing for interviews and realizing I cannot shake the habit of saying “we.”

When I talk about work I am proud of, I talk about what we built, what we changed, and what we figured out. The predictable next question from an interviewer is always: Yes, but what did you do?

Part of that habit is an aversion to self-promotion. But mostly, claiming individual credit for a complex outcome simply is not what happened. That is an experience I miss, and understanding what made it possible has become a benchmark for what I want to build next.

None of Us Knows Enough
#

Years later, working as a Scrum Master, I started reading research on effective teams and recognized something I had already lived.

What struck me was not how novel it sounded, but how familiar it felt: a shared goal, close interaction, an intuitive sense of what each person could bring, and the ability to work out an answer together. Those qualities had defined our small business-case team years earlier, long before I had the vocabulary for them.

The teams I served that worked best understood a premise (implicit or explicitly) that was comforting and simple:

None of us knows enough.

These were cross-functional teams, bringing different kinds of expertise to a shared problem. But what mattered was not just the mix of people. It was that the work required their contributions to affect one another. Assembled because the problem required knowledge that no single individual, and often no single discipline, could supply.

Difference was not an administrative nuisance to contain; it was the reason to assemble the team. It was not about a developer who failed to understand business, a designer who ignored engineering constraints, or a specialist who arrived after the interesting work was finished just to test what had been built. It was about what those different perspectives could build together.

Often the most valuable talent was an ability to notice what the rest of us missed.

Their background, their judgment, or their way of seeing a problem could fundamentally alter what the team thought it was doing. An operational constraint might reshape the design. The revised design might eliminate an expensive technical dependency. A business question might reveal that we were solving the wrong problem entirely.

The value was in those contributions colliding while it was still easy to change direction.

Shared Understanding, Not Shared Sameness
#

Organizational literature often talks about “shared mental models” as the foundation of team coordination. Do we understand what we are trying to achieve, how the moving pieces fit together, and what we can reasonably expect from one another?

On a healthy team, knowing that a colleague once worked in a different role is more than an interesting fact. It changes who we consult, what risks we anticipate, and how we approach new problems. Each person brings more than their title, and if the group understands enough about each member they can put that depth to work. Shared understanding does not mean everyone knows the exact same things; it means our different skills have somewhere functional to meet.

It also means no single leader needs to hold the entire answer. A manager can hold responsibility for overall direction without pretending to have the domain depth to resolve every trade-off alone. The team ought to take collective responsibility for coordinating activities, solving problems, and evaluating how it operates.

This model is not just better in the moment; it is resilient over time. The UK government’s doctrine on organizational resilience captures this when defining what a common purpose in a resilient organization should look like: leaders must “communicate and reinforce the importance of collaboration and a ‘beyond silos’ mindset in working towards the achievement of the organisation’s essential outcomes.”

At team level, when we understand what we are trying to accomplish and what each person can contribute, we have a basis for changing how we work when circumstances change. If we only understand our narrow, assigned lanes, we can produce our best work for a solution long after it has stopped making sense.

Shared understanding includes how we expect the work to happen, not just what we produce. And committing to that inevitably leads to conversations nobody particularly wants to have.

The Compromise Cannot Be One-Way
#

I once worked with a team where the default instinct was private incubation. Colleagues preferred to keep their ideas close, spend time developing them independently, and bring them to the table once they felt complete.

My instinct is the exact opposite. I rarely know what to fully think about a problem until we can put an idea on the board, test it through debate, pull it apart, and discard it without hurt feelings if the logic is weak.

To me, bringing a rough idea early was an act of collaboration. To them, it felt like reckless noise. Worse, questioning an idea I had held for ten minutes felt to me like open dialogue; questioning an idea they had worked on for three days felt like a challenge to their competence. By the time their concepts reached the room, days of personal effort had already been invested. Scrutinizing the premise meant asking someone to scrap a week of work. The room grew defensive. We were negotiating around finished, hardened positions when we could have been shaping unfinished thoughts together.

I had to examine my own costs, too. A fast, confident explanation can consume all the oxygen in a room before someone else has even formed their thought. What I experienced as open exploration could land on others as an aggressive, settled position.

Yet, over time, the expectation of adjustment became a one-way street. An implied moral hierarchy emerged: quiet hesitation was treated as inherently thoughtful and humble, while a desire for direct engagement was treated as an abrasive habit that needed to be tempered.

Slowing down was a reasonable request, but it was only half an answer. Without getting engagement back, alternative concepts, and active debate we had no shared mental model. We just had individuals waiting their turn to speak and not engaging with the ideas of their peers. Meetings felt like they could have been an email.

Eventually, I addressed the dynamic directly:

“I am willing to take leaps toward your style, but I need you to take steps toward mine.”

Not every thought had to be spoken immediately. But we needed enough exchange that silence did not leave us guessing whether people were reflecting, disagreeing, or waiting for their turn to share a disconnected piece of work.

It was uncomfortable, but it worked. Colleagues began bringing rough thoughts to the table. They challenged my proposals in real time, filling the pauses that I had previously rushed to fill with repetitive explanations. We had more room to alter direction before changing an idea meant undoing days of private effort.

We did not improve by deciding whose temperament was better. We were taking responsibility for how the team worked, not just what it delivered. Making an agreement about how our different ways of thinking could meet

Pocket Ready Rules
#

While I have spent hours stewing over these thoughts, in a few weeks, the details will fade. However, a few punchy phrases, a repeatable mantra or a punchy quote have the stickiness to be there when needed.

As I look ahead at the future, the environments I want to build, and the teams, products, and projects I want to take on, these are the sticky lines stand out through this reflection:

Difference needs somewhere to go

It will always exist, but without a constructive channel, it can settle into quiet cynicism, hallway complaints, and defensive silos. Brought into the open early, difference is a benefit. A room without friction isn’t aligned; it is just quiet.

Nobody knows enough

In work that is novel, complex and requires learning to do, the goal is never to be the smartest person at the table, but to ensure the table is smarter than any one person sitting at it. If one competency can solve a problem alone, the rest of the room is expensive overhead. In cross-functional teams we are not assembled to protect narrow jurisdictions or complete parallel tasks in isolation.

Truth has to come from debate, not an organizational chart

Hierarchy can allocate a budget, set a broad mandate, and carry the final accountability, but it cannot manufacture insight. Good environments are ones where arguments are tested on their merits, where half-formed thinking is invited in while the clay is wet, and where challenging an assumption is recognized as engagement not insubordination.

New information is never an inconvenient penalty

Discovering a flaw in the plan should not feel like an attack on someone’s competence or a burden that ruins days of work. It is what makes the result resilient. Spotting a design flaw or a missed constraint early in a project is not wasted effort; it is an early escape from an expensive failure. Discovering an error is simply the price of making contact with reality.

The most rewarding work is work where “we” is not a polite substitution for “I.”

It is an accurate description of how the outcome came to exist: not one strong individual with a supporting cast, and not a group of isolated contributors executing assignments in separate lanes. It is a group producing something that required what each person brought, where those contributions changed one another, and where the answer could never have existed in pieces.

Managing genuine difference is uncomfortable. It requires us to sit in the tension of the unresolved without rushing to force an artificial consensus. It asks us to slow down our tempo to let a colleague form a thought, while simultaneously expecting more methodical thinkers to bring their ideas forward before it is too late to change direction.

I have come to accept that regardless of formal title, I cannot simply tuck my own differences away and remain a passive participant. It shows up in picking up the whiteboard marker first to give an ambiguous problem a shape people can respond to, or physically rearranging the tables and chairs before a meeting so nobody is stranded outside the circle.

For those of us who share that desire to leave impacts where we go, we cannot disconnect from it for long. Finding, building and holding onto the rewarding environments that produce the best work will require coming back to how they emerged and the craft of curating our best ideas and practice will continue.

entry.title: Seeing the Difference Between a Boss and a Botanist
entry.summary: In the sclerosis of corporate hierarchies, middle management often finds itself caricatured as a relic of bygone organizational structures, scar tissue left behind by the Peter Principle. From the bumbling inefficiency of Office Space’s Lumbergh to the clichéd “paper-pusher,” middle managers have been the subject…
entry.content:
In the sclerosis of corporate hierarchies, middle management often finds itself caricatured as a relic of bygone organizational structures, scar tissue left behind by the Peter Principle. From the bumbling inefficiency of Office Space’s Lumbergh to the clichéd “paper-pusher,” middle managers have been the subject of fascination, frustration, and ridicule. But these stereotypes belie a deeper truth: middle managers, especially in knowledge work are essential stewards of an organizations most important and undervalued resource: the team.

From my experience as an Agile coach, I have seen firsthand how strong middle management can transform teams. When managers embrace a servant-leadership mindset — prioritizing the needs of their teams over the impulse to dictate outcomes — their teams flourish. Psychological safety increases, innovation thrives, and organizations become more resilient. Conversely, poor middle management can create bottlenecks, stifle creativity, and cause disengagement, ultimately leading to attrition and stagnation.

Organizations that undervalue middle managers risk missing out on their most significant leverage points for change. Leadership teams set the vision, but it is middle management that makes change stick. The bravest among them create feedback loops to share the “ground-truth” that leaders could never see. The real work of organizational transformation — whether it be cultural shifts, Agile adoption, or strategic pivots — lives in the day-to-day decisions and interactions managed at the working level.

When innovation originates at the team level and complexity outstrips top-down decision-making, the question isn’t whether middle management is relevant. The question is how the role can work to meet the evolving needs of organizations. This evolution requires us to think of middle management not as a title but as a discipline — a practice rooted in enabling others, fostering collaboration, and shaping environments where knowledge and creativity thrive.

From Title to Discipline: Middle Managers as Ecosystem Architects

For much of the 20th century, leadership was synonymous with expertise. Managers were the chess masters, moving pieces with precision, assumed to be the most knowledgeable in the room. But in today’s dynamic work environments, that model is can’t stay true. Innovation and knowledge creation now reside at the team level, where the people closest to the work hold the most up-to-date insights. After all, they are the ones creating and interpreting that knowledge. Through experimentation, incremental work, and reflection, teams refine their contributions in real time.

This shift leaves middle managers on the outside. If knowledge is created at the team level, managers simply can’t be the best informed. Their distance from the work makes this impossible. If they can no longer be the most informed decision-makers or technical experts, where can they add the most value?

This shift redefines the manager’s role from that of a directive authority to an “ecosystem architect,” someone who cultivates the conditions for innovation and collaboration to flourish. Middle managers are not here to dictate; they are here to build. They assemble diverse teams, foster the kinds of teams that dive deep together to uncover new ways to solve hard problems, and create an environment where collective intelligence can thrive.

As architects, middle managers can bridge the micro realities of team dynamics with the macro vision of organizational strategy. They are stewards of the processes, relationships, and cultures that transform individual effort into collective success. They don’t just enforce rules; they design systems that enable creativity and resilience. They act as gardeners of the ecosystem. Just as a gardener can’t will a plant to grow, they can control the environment and selection of plants.

Leadership as Gardening: Cultivating High-Performing Teams

The idea of leadership as gardening is perhaps best illustrated by U.S. General Stanley McChrystal, who famously redefined leadership during his time commanding the Joint Special Operations Task Force in Iraq. Faced with the fast-evolving landscapes of asymmetric guerrilla warfare, McChrystal realized that traditional, hierarchical command structures were insufficient. His leadership team had to evolve from a ground-war command style to one of distributed decision-making and adaptability.

McChrystal’s approach emphasized the need to cultivate environments where informed decisions could be made at all levels. Similarly, effective middle managers enable teams to adapt, innovate, and thrive in complex, dynamic environments — though surely with significantly less immediate stakes.

In organizations where ideas are the most valuable resource, middle managers act as gardeners nurturing thriving ecosystems. Middle managers, as gardeners of organizational ecosystems, take on a craft-oriented role, carefully shaping teams, processes, cultures, and norms to foster sustainable growth and innovation. Gardening is not passive; it requires intentional effort to balance competing priorities and ensure the ecosystem thrives as a whole.

Just as a gardener must weed out invasive plants that threaten the harmony of the garden, middle managers address behaviours or dynamics that disrupt team cohesion or effectiveness. They prune back certain aspects of processes or team interactions to create space for others to flourish, knowing that overgrowth in one area can overshadow critical contributions elsewhere. Similarly, they choose what to plant — assembling teams with diverse, complementary skills, perspectives, and strengths. This deliberate curation ensures that the soil of the team — its collective intelligence — is enriched and balanced, promoting long-term health and productivity.

Cultivating Psychological Safety

More important than anything else, middle managers must cultivate psychological safety within their teams. As Amy Edmondson emphasizes in her book Teaming, this involves fostering an environment where team members feel comfortable taking risks, voicing concerns, and learning from mistakes without fear of judgment or retribution.

This isn’t merely about avoiding blame or punishment but about shaping the very dynamics of how the team operates. Think of it like a game of strategic interaction. In a traditional, hierarchical setting, the default strategy for team members might be to prioritize self-preservation. Challenging a flawed idea or proposing a radical solution carries significant risks: potential embarrassment, social ostracization, or even career damage. The “payoff” for this risk-averse behavior is minimal — maintaining the status quo, avoiding conflict, and ensuring personal safety.

This dynamic mirrors Rousseau’s classic Stag Hunt. In this scenario, a group of hunters can either cooperate to hunt a large stag, providing a bountiful feast for all, or individually hunt for hares, guaranteeing a smaller but certain meal. If all hunters cooperate and focus on the stag, they achieve the optimal outcome. However, if even one hunter defects and pursues a hare, the stag will escape, leaving all with only meagre rabbit meat (which if hunters eat exclusively, they will perish from what is known a rabbit starvation).

In the absence of a shared understanding of the collective goal and a culture of trust and mutual support, individual self-interest often prevails. Team members, fearing the potential consequences of challenging the status quo or taking risks, opt for the safe option — pursuing individual goals or maintaining the status quo. This leads to a suboptimal outcome for the entire team, hindering innovation, stifling creativity, and ultimately limiting the team’s ability to achieve its full potential.

By cultivating a culture of psychological safety, middle managers can shift the game. They can raise the potential rewards for challenging the status quo while simultaneously lowering the negative consequences. This creates a virtuous cycle where:

  • Challenging ideas becomes the expected norm: Team members are encouraged to question assumptions, offer constructive criticism, and engage in open debate.
  • Collective intelligence flourishes: Diverse perspectives are valued, and the team leverages the combined knowledge and creativity of its members to achieve better outcomes.
  • Learning and innovation thrive: A culture of experimentation and learning from both successes and failures becomes embedded in the team’s DNA.

The Practical Value of Middle Management

By consciously shaping the social and interpersonal dynamics within their teams and cultivating a culture of trust and openness, middle managers can unlock the full potential of their teams and drive high performance.

Beyond assembling the right people and cultivating psychological safety, middle managers also:

  • Facilitate continuous learning: They create opportunities for reflection, experimentation, and knowledge sharing within and across teams. This might involve organizing workshops, team retrospectives, or knowledge-sharing sessions.
  • Build and maintain team networks: Middle managers help their teams connect with other teams, departments, and external stakeholders, fostering collaboration and access to diverse perspectives.
  • Adapt to changing circumstances: In today’s dynamic environment, middle managers must be agile and adaptable, supporting their teams as they navigate uncertainty and adjust to new challenges.

In this ecosystem, the manager’s role is not to dictate but to facilitate. They encourage cross-pollination of ideas by connecting teams across silos, ensuring that insights flow freely throughout the organization. They also act as guardians of focus, shielding their teams from unnecessary distractions while keeping them aligned with strategic priorities.

Investing in Teams: Lessons from Google

This is not simply a well-meaning or moral idea; it has real implications for organizational success. For example, tech companies like Google show us how valuable cohesive teams are in the knowledge economy. Their billion-dollar acquisitions aren’t just about technology — they’re about acquiring the brilliant teams behind that technology. When Google buys a firm like Raxium, it’s not just snapping up a product; it’s also bringing in the people who built it. A $1 billion purchase of a 50-person team? That’s $20 million per employee — proof that they value the people as much as, if not more than, the product itself.

Google’s approach to acquisitions reflects a mindset shift. They know that the expertise and creativity of a well-honed team are invaluable. Breezometer, for instance, wasn’t acquired solely for its air quality monitoring service. Even after shutting the product down, Google integrated the team’s knowledge into services like Google Maps. It’s not about the widget; it’s about the people behind it.

Conclusion: The Future of Middle Management

Middle management is not a relic of the past but an essential pillar of modern organizations. As knowledge work becomes more complex and dynamic, the role of middle managers must evolve accordingly. Their value lies not in control, but in cultivation — shaping the conditions that enable teams to thrive, adapt, and innovate.

The most effective middle managers are not bureaucratic bottlenecks but ecosystem architects, balancing autonomy with alignment and fostering environments where collective intelligence flourishes. They facilitate learning, remove obstacles, and build the connective tissue that allows organizations to harness the full potential of their people.

Far from being obsolete, middle management is more critical than ever. The organizations that recognize this — and invest in developing managers as enablers of high-performing teams — will be the ones that navigate complexity and change with the greatest agility. The future of work will not be shaped by rigid hierarchies, but by those who understand that leadership is less about directing and more about designing the right conditions for success. Hopefully with great mutual respect between themselves and agile coaches / scrum masters (the author wrote with no hidden personal agenda.)

entry.title: From Shovels to Software: Why Difference Matters When Things Get Complex
entry.summary: In many creative activities the medium of execution is intractable. Lumber splits; paints smear; electrical circuits ring. These physical limitations of the medium constrain the ideas that may be expressed, and they also create unexpected difficulties in the implementation. Implementation, then, takes time and sweat…
entry.content:
In many creative activities the medium of execution is intractable. Lumber splits; paints smear; electrical circuits ring. These physical limitations of the medium constrain the ideas that may be expressed, and they also create unexpected difficulties in the implementation.

Implementation, then, takes time and sweat both because of the physical media and because of the inadequacies of the underlying ideas. We tend to blame the physical media for most of our implementation difficulties; for the media are not “ours” in the way the ideas are, and our pride colors our judgment.

- “The Mythical Man Month” — Fred Brooks, 1975

In the nearly half century since Fred Brooks articulated the idea of a “mythical man month,” the myth persists. He attributed the myth to optimism, that software development is a “modern sorcery

\[that\]

especially attracts those who believe in happy endings and fairy godmothers.”

The persistent mythology, that if we close our eyes, and think hard enough, that we can put together a perfectly tractable plan of what we want to build, how we can build it and who will need to pull it together, is an optimistic delusion. This optimism has real consequences, and I’ve witnessed language used by those concerned with diversity that reflects this as a foundation for some of their resistance to accepting diversity and inclusion not simply as a moral imperative, but as a benefit to improved performance.

In today’s ever changing and interconnected world, organizations are facing the challenge of complex work environments. More and more work is shifting from the complicated (difficult to fully grasp, but possible to learn over time) to the complex (highly interdependent and variable). Through this, I’ll make an effort to draw lines from complexity, management theory and diversity together into a mental model to add context to the relationship between diversity, inclusion, and collaboration in the context of complex work.

The Complicated and the Complex
#

As a starting point for moving further, I have to start with a few definitions.

  • We’ll take the idea of a “simple” problem as one in which there is a single optimal peak; the optimal weight of a shovel-full of coal to unload a cart in a 12 hour shift.
  • A complicated problem where there may be multiple “good” solutions and one “optimal” solution but once they are discovered through training and experience, they remain optimal. Imagine watch repair, there are multiple strategies for diagnosis and repair, but with enough experience a repair-person can find at least a personal (local) optimum.
  • And finally, the complex and chaotic environments of the dancing landscapes, in which optimums can only temporarily be discovered, a peak today may not be a peak tomorrow, an optimum may not be an optimum in a year, etc. An easy example would be financial markets, where any sufficiently good strategy, ceases to be a good strategy once other parties wise up to it (Adaptive Market Hypothesis).

Kicking and Screaming Into Complexity
#

Regardless of how we choose to encode the ideas of complexity, either the above, or other common models like Cynefin, the key idea is that there is a point in complexity where we leave the world of the predictable, stable and solvable and enter a different domain.

When we traverse across that line, we have to discard many notions that worked in the predictable environment. Best practices become good practices, the very notion that a single practice can be best is a fools errand. Processes become anchors slowing down needed change. Staying still becomes as big a risk as changing, where adaptability is a dimension of organizational resilience (see BS 65000:2022 — Organizational Resilience).

All models are wrong, some are useful. — George Box, 1976

Amidst the ever-evolving landscape of modern work dynamics the model at hand may indeed falter in numerous aspects, no model will ever be perfect. However, at the heart of this idea lies a pivotal concept: a tipping point where the realm of work is no longer defined by the comfort of predictability, but by the challenges of unpredictability. A paradigm shift that encourages us to re-calibrate our approach. Embracing this metaphoric fault line between divergent landscapes is a challenge.

Sensing Complexity
#

It’s easy to see when it’s on a diagram but how can we sense when we’re working in a complex environment? There is no clear line between the two ideas in real life, with problems don’t come with a label. Some problems have puzzled mathematicians for years with no solution that seem easy but have no solution: the moving sofa problem (What is the largest area of a shape that can be maneuvered through a unit-width L-shaped corridor?) as an example, has no solution.

In Nassim Nicolas Taleb’s Antifragile he offers some indicators that a system is complex. That complex systems are characterized by intricate interdependencies and nonlinear responses. In these systems, doubling a factor does not result in a proportional doubling of the effect but rather an amplified or diminished impact. Simple cause-and-effect relationships do not hold, and understanding the functioning of individual parts alone is insufficient.

And so, we go full circle. The opening quote of this writing from the Mythical Man-Month, exemplifies this non-linearity. The conclusion that adding more developers to a late project tends to make them later, is a great indicator that software development, and likely all similarly intangible knowledge work, is complex, not simple or complicated. The rest of the writing will use software development and knowledge work generally, as marquee examples in comparison to other clearly simple or complicated types of work.

Diversity as a Tool in Knowledge Work
#

Knowledge workers are persons who understand their job better than their boss — Peter Drucker

If we are to accept that:

  • Knowledge work is complex and requires teams of skilled people working together
  • Complex work is unpredictable, interconnected and non-linear
  • The necessary tools required to or expertise to achieve positive results won’t be predictable (at least over a sufficient time space)

Then surely the natural response would be to seek not to build a team of “qualified” individuals who fit the same mould. Instead, an approach could be to optimize for the broadest germane skills and tools. Diversity of thought, over convergence to a mean.

Below is a very simplified model built to illustrate some key difference between; making the complicated workings of a watch and the complex development of a novel software product.

Some key difference that might be visible:

The table above almost certainly sells the incredible skills of watchmaking short, but as a model, the key ideas hopefully hold up. The key concepts that we can tease out though are:

  • The outcome of work; the product, requires collaboration between team members with multiple skills where individual contribution alone cannot produce value
  • The skills needed to complete work usually require a breadth of skills and knowledge beyond a single individual’s capacity; a typical flow of requirements, design, implement, test and deploy may require all of the roles in the diagram to work together
  • The relationship between the team and the work isn’t predictable, some work may require a large amount of design, some may require extremely in-depth knowledge of development or knowledge of a new business domain.

Unpredictability in work, needed skills/knowledge and the inter-connectedness of a individuals on a team mean that a viable strategy to strengthen a team is to pursue adding to existing skills, but also add diverse perspectives and heuristics. A team might look at what upcoming work is coming and ask themselves what perspectives are missing to address the work.

Say this team had to balance two very big pieces of work in their system: a large security issue and a challenging high priority feature request. What could they do as a first step? Look at the new work and ask themselves, what they might be missing to address them, and seek out adding that to the team. It is only the team though who could assess this as it is based on their collective skills.

Let’s assume the team looks inward and decides they need to add a new member to address these two needs. It’s likely they come to a conclusion that the new member should not have the same background as themselves. Additionally, if they foresee that future work will require this same bringing in of new knowledge, then the optimal approach of who to bring in is to bring someone in who looks like the least like them with the most different perspectives and heuristics.

Cognitive diversity builds their capacity to address the problems of today and better position themselves to address problems in the future.

Sympathy for the Devil
#

When I imagine a worker spending all day shovelling coal, seeing their daily pay and seeing a smaller pile of coal next to theirs done by another worker paid the same it doesn’t feel like a stretch to imagine the discontentment they may feel. The same might be felt by a craftsman who built a watch (or more watches) of higher quality than a peer who also was paid the same. In these environments, perhaps some discontentment that a “diversity hire” could be brought in may feel a little more justified.

However, when looking at knowledge work, where complexity is the norm, how can we justify that same sentiment? I’d argue that we simply can’t. The volatility, uncertainty, complexity, and ambiguity of the work environment ought to compel teams to add skills different from their own as a route to making themselves and their teams better. Holding onto notions of strict “qualifications” serve to limit the pool of perspectives and tools that teams may have access to. Certainly, there’s a need to retain germane skills but when work requires increasing breadth of knowledge can we reasonably expect to address new challenges by bringing in people who look, act and work just like us?

entry.title: Building a Trade-off Mentality
entry.summary: If you wish to make an apple pie from scratch, you must first invent the universe. – Carl Sagan Carl Sagan’s famous quote inspires deeper thought of how connected our universe is, that to “make an apple pie from scratch” you can keep going one…
entry.content:
If you wish to make an apple pie from scratch, you must first invent the universe.
– Carl Sagan

Carl Sagan’s famous quote inspires deeper thought of how connected our universe is, that to “make an apple pie from scratch” you can keep going one step backwards until one has to “invent the universe.” What struck me was, that somewhere between the start of the universe and baking the pie, we had to draw a line for what we consider “from scratch.” Why would buying pre-made pie crust feel like “cheating,” yet buying pre-ground flour would not? What lines have we drawn without much thought of how we choose them?

Let’s imagine a manager asking someone to take on a new task. Consider the assumptions that may be at play: the manager assumes the employee can do the task, will listen, will understand, and could do the work without sacrificing their current efforts. What trade-offs are involved? What work might suffer to focus on this new task? How would the manager or the employee differ in their views of what could be dropped to accommodate the new work and what might those different opinions tell us about what each of them values?

I’ve found it useful to ask myself what assumptions I’m making when I make a statement. This approach helps me identify what trade-offs and assumed truths may need to be evaluated to see if they’re still true. However, within my head, I can take a far more confrontational approach to my thoughts than I may with others. Thus, I worked on trying out a more inquisitive approach using a mental toolkit that I call the “trade-off mentality” as a way to more collaboratively uncover inbuilt assumptions and have open discussions about the underlying rationale behind our decisions, preferences and assumptions.

While I do believe this is a general toolkit that has helped me think better across multiple domains, the focus in the text below will be largely on software development and teams.

This mental toolkit is based on four core ideas:

  • First, there ain’t no such thing as a free lunch — we cannot simply get something without giving something up.
  • Second, trade-offs allow us to question what we value.
  • Third, trade-offs offer an opportunity for us to discuss ways of splitting or breaking down things we bundle together or associate.
  • Finally, when we evaluate decisions and assumptions, we can gain additional insight by asking ourselves who is being served by balancing and weighing valuations.

Idea 1: There ain’t no such thing as a free lunch
#

Central to the first idea is the acknowledgement that all endeavours entail a cost and are bound by constraints. That we cannot get a “free lunch.” Choosing to stay up late to watch another episode of Succession, means accepting you might be a little tired tomorrow. We are constrained by time, energy, money, and many other limits.

For instance, we can look at even subtle constraints to a team’s productivity. My favourite to consider is the cognitive load incurred by increasing work complexity (or simply using the idea of mental energy). Such complexity may hinder growth, or necessitate trade-offs in terms of longer learning, more challenging onboarding, or higher rates of incidents. Surfacing impacts from complexity could help identify future challenges and uncover risks we might not be willing to accept.

Indicator statements such as: “We should make time for training,” “I would like you to deliver this as well,” or “The team must assume accountability for this new system” may serve as potential triggers for conversations on underlying assumptions and required trade-offs. The figure below shows a hypothetical model of transition for a team taking on a new application, in which a new idea comes to mind — the “cost” of assuming new accountabilities.

Team Capacity During a Transition

There ain't no such thing as a free lunch. Adding work means something else gets less capacity.

This figure needs JavaScript. The gist: before a transition the team spends most capacity on the critical system with room for training, while in the first year of transition a new application takes half of capacity and both core work and training shrink.

0%
Before Transition
Before

After
Critical System

Pushes out core work. Down from 80% to 40% to make room for the new system.

New Low Availability Application
50%

This new load is the tradeoff. It takes half of capacity, squeezing out development of people and product.

Training & Development

Less room to improve. Halved from 20% to 10%, so the team has less capacity to develop its people and its product over the long run.

Team Capacity Allocation

A classic trade-off in systems development, for example, is the balance between investing in new features versus reducing technical debt. A team’s ability to discuss and evaluate these classic trade-offs can have a significant impact on their long-term success. Investments in technical debt reduction, while not as glamorous as new features, can often lead to more sustainable development and increased capacity for future innovation.

By carefully examining statements, especially those that indicate a “more X” is possible, we can surface implicit assumptions and trade-offs, while individuals and teams can better understand the consequences of their decisions and align their actions with their values and goals.

Idea 2: Trade-off decisions offer a space to inspect values
#

When confronted with a potential trade-off, we have a space to ask ourselves, “Why did I choose X over Y?” Is that choice consistent with my values? With a team’s values? With an organization’s goals?

The act of questioning myself has helped me gain insight into my own beliefs and assumptions. When considering whether to speak up in a group setting, for instance, I consider if I am preventing someone else from contributing or if simply presenting an opinion may discourage dissenting viewpoints. Even the subtle act of supporting an idea may make dissenting viewpoints harder to bring forward.

When faced with a difficult decision, individuals may engage in a process of introspection, carefully evaluating the relative importance of the available options and the factors that inform those values. This process can be particularly valuable in group settings where individuals with different skill sets and viewpoints must navigate trade-offs to achieve a common goal.

But, evaluating trade-offs is not just an individual activity. Teams and organizations can also benefit from examining the trade-offs they make in pursuit of their goals. By holding up a mirror to themselves and asking if they are truly living up to their values, teams can identify areas for improvement and develop strategies to better align their actions with their goals. For example, a team tasked with reporting weekly on their progress may be trading off valuable development time and energy for the sake of reporting. By examining this trade-off, the team could question which benefits of reporting outweigh the costs and adjust their approach accordingly.

This particular idea may be more difficult to have an open dialogue about because it may challenge deeply held assumptions. Two areas I have had difficult discussions about have been the topics of reporting and options analysis. If we believe our value is to deliver work and support clients/customers/users, both would be “wastes” from a Lean perspective. Options analysis embeds a guarantee of waste; that if N+1 options are presented and 1 option is selected the development of N was largely waste. Softer language, of relative value and checking against objectives, helps serve a less aggressive proposition.

Similarly, organizations with a mission to be inclusive may need to examine the trade-offs between objective hiring criteria and the desire to attract a more diverse pool of candidates. Organizations could dig deeper into whether they are truly living up to their values and identify ways to make their processes more equitable and inclusive. Perhaps recognizing that adhering to a strict process may reduce the impact of individual biases while amplifying the impact of structural ones. e.g. a hiring process that takes 3 months to complete, requires a masters degree and 10 years previous experience excludes the population of people who can’t wait 3 months for a new career and don’t have equitable access to the educational and experience requirements.

Ultimately, by carefully evaluating the trade-offs we can support, individuals, organizations and teams have more informed decisions and work towards achieving their goals with greater clarity and purpose.

Idea 3: Try to unwrap packages
#

One other technique that has been useful when evaluating trade-offs is to do what I have called unwrapping packages. The idea behind this is to unwrap, unbundle and uncouple to make more honest decisions about trade-offs. In the rest of this section, I’ll focus on particular patterns I have found useful to key in on common “bundlings.”

One such pattern is association. This pattern involves examining implicit connections we make between ideas. For example, we might assume that working in an office is essential for building strong social connections. While there may be some truth to this, it’s important to recognize that there are other ways to foster social connections. By breaking down these associations we can have more a balanced discussion. In the case of working in an office, the trade-off is not simply between having social connections and staying at home. Instead, it’s about the ease of building connections when we are physically together versus the additional effort required to do so when working remotely.

In this example, we change the discussion from “work from home” vs “connect with new colleagues,” to “work from home and have a more difficult time connecting with new colleagues” vs “go to the office where the friction between meeting new people is lower.” This can support a more nuanced decision, where we can open up dialogue on, for example:

  • How to support remote colleagues to form new connections?
  • Why does being in the office encourage more connections and if moving around the building is an important factor, how can we offer that same benefit to less mobile colleagues?

In the world of project management, the concept of a “work package” is all about bundling tasks together into work packages or projects themselves. This approach can be useful in certain situations, particularly when it comes to managing large-scale investments. After all, the bigger the package, the greater the economies of scale that can be achieved (investment governance tends to be roughly equal effort regardless of project sizes).

However, there are also cases where this approach might be detrimental. In situations where a team is stable, and tools and solutions are already in place, breaking down tasks into smaller packages can be more effective. This allows for greater flexibility in addressing high-priority items, regardless of where they might fit into a larger package.

Bundling vs Unbundling Work

If critical work is bundled with low-priority work, it might wait for the whole package. Breaking it apart lets it jump to the front.

This figure needs JavaScript. The gist: bundled work forces low priority items in Project 1 ahead of higher value work elsewhere, while unbundling lets the critical item go first.

Critical
High Value
Medium
Low Priority

Critical Piece of Work
Low Importance Bug-Fix
Low Importance UI Update
Project 2 High value
High Value Enhancement

High Value Enhancement

Medium Risk Security Fix

Done first, ahead of the rest. High value work in Project 2 and the security fix in Project 3 move up next.

To illustrate this point, let’s consider an abstract example. Imagine that there are three potential packages of work and one of them contains critical work. There’s no question that this work should take priority over all other work. However, if this critical work is bundled with other non-critical work, the entire package might be completed before other packages containing high-priority work. In this scenario, the lower-priority work ends up taking precedence simply because it was packaged together with the critical work. By breaking work down into smaller, more manageable pieces, teams can avoid this issue and ensure that the most important work always takes priority.

While on the subject of processes, another common pattern is historical linkage; rules and procedures that persist even if they are no longer relevant or useful. For example, some project methodologies require consultation with a vendor or asset management team as a precaution against licensing overages and legal risks. While this may have made sense in the past, with the rise of cloud technology, the need for such consultations is much lower (with software included in the service offering). However, because of the long-standing association between vendor management and licensing, this may be embedded as a required step for going live with delivery even though the previous risk has subsided.

Idea 4: Who is being served?
#

Finally, and usually done in concert with the above ideas, is to look at “who is being served” by a choice.

I recall years ago during the transition from an older platform for document management to a newer one, I was part of a group to decide what the folder structure ought to be for projects and support teams. The facilitator in the discussion walked in with the assumption that we needed to have the same structure for everyone. This assumption certainly made sense for their project, once defined it could be copied and pasted for everyone and they could move on. However, in representing teams’ needs the group had very different ideas of what worked best for them.

Seeing an opportunity to ask, I posed a question to the group on where this assumption was made. The conversation went a little something like this:

Facilitator: “We need to standardize folder structure so that when a team member joins from another project they can find documents.”

Me: “How often does it happen?”

Facilitator: “Maybe a couple of times a year”

Me: “Are we sure that designing a standard system to serve a twice-a-year event, over allowing the unique needs of teams and projects to be served is the best approach? When I’ve seen new team members join there’s usually been additional guidance provided, a “buddy system” usually, to help them orient themselves on what’s important. Wouldn’t that help serve that need?”

Others seemed to react positively to the idea and the discussion following was more positive. There is no current standard, but there is a “starting” template to get teams off on the right foot. We struck a better balance.

Another example was offered above, requests that may come for status reporting. It’s certainly understandable for leaders to want visibility into work. Yet, accepting that reporting doesn’t come for free and that when data on team performance “escapes” the team it costs the team safety to make changes — especially when an experiment might cause a temporary slowdown. Is it worth serving a leader’s need for observability over the potential drawbacks of lower team safety and less available time for work? Perhaps, but raising the discussion and balancing leadership’s need to work with their peers, stakeholders and other leaders allows for more nuance, especially for metrics that may influence team behaviours.

The classic adage of Goodheart’s Law : would state that “when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure.” An unfortunate example of this has occurred in hospitals in the UK where a focus on individual mortality rates for surgeons alters their behaviour with 1 in 3 surgeons reported avoiding difficult cases to protect their metrics . The trade-off we make when metrics escape, doesn’t mean we ought to avoid reporting, but that we should discuss what effects might come from them.

For those in software, there are well-established metrics available, colloquially called theDORA metrics , with years of research behind them. These metrics are described by Google as:

Deployment Frequency — How often an organization successfully releases to production

Lead Time for Changes — The amount of time it takes a commit to get into production

Change Failure Rate — The percentage of deployments causing a failure in production

Time to Restore Service — How long it takes an organization to recover from a failure in production

Wrap-Up
#

In environments where we are constantly making decisions, it’s easy to overlook the assumptions and trade-offs we make. The idea of a free lunch is a myth; everything we do comes at a cost. A trade-off mentality, informed by the four ideas above, has helped me have better conversations with others and better introspection. By acknowledging the constraints that underlie our systems, I feel better equipped to have constructive, open conversations.

While it’s been helpful for now to adopt a more inquisitive “trade-off mentality,” it’s still a work in progress. Through this lens, I work to support better dialogue. If you’re reading this, try it out the next time you are confronted with a difficult decision or hear a statement that “doesn’t sit right.” Remember to acknowledge that nothing comes for free and when we work in complex environments, we work best when we openly discuss our ideas and concerns. When you are brought into these discussions, challenge yourself to question “What’s the trade-off here?”

entry.title: Changing Requirements to be a Successful Business Analyst
entry.summary: A look into personal experience with business analysis, agile and modern projects. My first exposure to the business analyst role was at the Canadian Food Inspection Agency (CFIA), while working with a team focused on policy. While there, I was fortunate enough to involve myself…
entry.content:
A look into personal experience with business analysis, agile and modern projects.

My first exposure to the business analyst role was at the Canadian Food Inspection Agency (CFIA), while working with a team focused on policy. While there, I was fortunate enough to involve myself in other initiatives, giving me exposure to a new world of roles within the organization.

After being asked to help out in coordinating some projects I began work with the corporate planning office. The first meeting we had I was introduced to a role new to me, called a business analyst (BA).

Meeting this team of BAs, I felt a real connection to the role, that I could have a career in front of me. There was a real professional practice to what I felt was natural, but was ultimately novel in a policy world. That when working on an initiative we should have a clear vision for why we were doing it, what we hoped to resolve, and what success would look like. Business analysis offered a repeatable methodology for obtaining these answers.

The next initiative I began was towards the development of a standard operating procedures guide to navigate the Agency’s corporate policies and procedures. Throughout this work, there were innumerable “whys” I wanted to ask to bring context to the instructions. I felt drawn to provide background when expecting users to follow instructions. Context, I felt, was key in getting buy-in.

Always questioning the “why” behind a seemingly infinite abyss of process, I was particularly drawn to the process re-engineering elements of the task. I began to look for support from professional disciplines to my incessant probing. My research revealed that again, business analysis would help me apply some method my instincts.

Learning this, I sought to attain more formal education, leading me to sign up for a program offered jointly by Carleton and York Universities’ business schools. At this program I had the good fortune to learn from some early members in the founding of the International Institute of Business Analysis (IIBA) and some of the world’s first official Business Analysts.

They shared with the class that the reason they founded the IIBA and created the role was to support a clear value proposition: projects frequently fail and the most frequent cause was poor management of requirements. A role that directly addressed this problem would have a strong return on investment.

While in the formative years of the role, there were debates on title and responsibilities. Before settling on Business Analyst, a leading candidate was “Requirements Manager.” Along with the title the role would exist on par with the Project Manager, taking accountability for the scope of an initiative. When incomplete and changing requirements were showing up among the top reasons for project failures, the case was clear: managing requirements would reduce the risk of project failures and save millions in sunk costs.

This concept of formally managed “requirements” was new to me. They weren’t what had drawn me to the role, nor were they what the business analysts I first met were focused on. The work that the BAs were doing that drew me to the profession was much more focused on identifying the value to the organization and managing to fit it back in as development progressed.

What do I need to be successful?
#

Requirements in the traditional sense simply help define what an initiative needs to achieve to be successful. But there are a few issues with the concept:

  • They capture the best knowledge available at a point in time and rarely change; even worse they often reflect the best understanding of technology by non-technical users without having seen a system or prototype
  • They apply formality to what often would be better served as a conversation or dialogue
  • By investing time in documenting them and going through approvals, there is a sunk cost that makes it difficult to change
  • There is often resistance to changing them through existing project mechanisms, such as change control, even when new information is uncovered

These issues are similar to those that hamper the growth of the business analysis practice. The best knowledge available when the role was being created was that the majority of software development was occurring through projects, those projects were failing at an alarming rate (nearly 1/3 being cancelled) and that poor management of requirements was a significant contributor.

However, today, less than 20% of projects are cancelled and an increasingly large number of projects are being done in an Agile manner (in which only 9% of projects fail). In the most common Agile methodology, Scrum, there is no specific Business Analyst role. The wild west of projects looks to be maturing, finding new ways to be successful without the tools of projects past.

What this tells us is a story of a core skill-set that is languishing, yet the role is growing:

The title moved from the work to the worker

Monthly Google Trends interest for three English-language geographies. Each geography scales separately, so compare shapes, not heights.

This figure needs JavaScript. The gist: in Canada the analyst title led from 2004 and pulled further ahead after 2019, while interest in the activity itself stayed roughly flat.

What makes us successful?
#

The role of the business analyst has become increasingly common in organizations and looking to grow (in the US an expected 14% growth from 2014 to 2024). What are they doing if they aren’t focused on what we used to call “business analysis?”

From personal experience, I have seen a shift from when I started working as a Business Analyst in 2011. When I began, I was working on one of the last major initiatives managed with strict requirements traceability, focused on stringent use cases and detailed requirements. Artifacts that feel like relics today.

Throughout the project, I never felt the like the work I did was really adding value to the end users. Instead it felt more akin to writing a dictionary, something that would never be read as a whole but referenced if we encountered a word we didn’t understand. This wasn’t valuable to the people who needed a new system to do their jobs. Sure it was potentially valuable to investment governance, audit and project management if something went wrong. But choosing to focus on potential value for potential stakeholders over real users was foolhardy.

The core focus of my work was to reduce the drift of the project from an objective set at a point with the least information in the project life-cycle. Even worse, to produce work that would make course correction more costly.

What felt the most valuable was not the work I was supposed to be focused on. Instead, I found that the most rewarding work fit into two areas; ensuring that the project “fit” into the organization and leveraging soft skills like facilitation and consensus building to connect the many parties involved and help them understand the complexities behind decisions.

The modern analyst trades depth for range

Representative scale of expected skill level.

This figure needs JavaScript. The gist: the traditional profile peaks at Requirements Management, the modern profile peaks at organizational fit and soft skills.

Managing requirements in the traditional methodologies only added complexity. I distinctly remember looking at project with 500+ discrete requirements and thinking to myself; “how can anybody possibly be sure these are still true?” The “modern” Business Analyst has value, and is most valuable when they are contributing their skill-set to work that helps the organization navigate itself through the endless sea of change on the horizon.

The role of Business Analyst has a lot to contribute, but it’s most valuable when we can balance the interests of a project with the interests of the organization. In finding that balance, the role of Business Analyst returns to a clear value proposition. To do what the role has historically done well at, provide the organization an interface to support changes inside and out.

Business analysis as a practice dedicated to managing requirements is on its way out. However, business analysis has a much brighter future if it can address the complexity of systems, organizations, and their use of technology. It can also take the soft skills that have always been core to successfully managing requirements — e.g. consensus building, facilitation and negotiation — to modern development practices.
